paragraphs.heading: Standing in for a thermometer
paragraphs.text: Reliable global records of climate go back only to the 1880s. To learn about climate before that, scientists turn to climate proxies. These are preserved physical, chemical and biological features of the past that take the place of direct measurements. Proxies are the only means scientists have of working out climate patterns from before record-keeping began.

paragraphs.heading: The idea behind a proxy
paragraphs.text: Sometimes science has to study a quantity that cannot be measured directly. A proxy method measures something else that correlates with that quantity, and then uses it to infer the value that is wanted. This approach is especially useful for past climate, in the times before direct temperature measurements are available.

paragraphs.heading: Many kinds of evidence
paragraphs.text: Proxies have been studied in a variety of geological settings. Among them are measurements of stable isotopes in ice cores, the growth rates of tree rings, the mix of pollen species in lake sediment, temperature profiles of boreholes, and the isotopes and minerals of corals. In each case the indicator was shaped by one particular seasonal feature of climate, such as summer temperature or monsoon intensity, when it was laid down or grew.

paragraphs.heading: Calibrating a proxy
paragraphs.text: Most proxy records have to be calibrated. They are compared with independent temperature measurements, or with another proxy that has been calibrated more directly, over the period when the two overlap. That gives an estimate of how the proxy relates to temperature. The proxy's longer history is then used to reconstruct temperatures from earlier periods. Interpreting proxies also calls for cross-checking one indicator against others.

paragraphs.heading: What ice cores hold
paragraphs.text: Ice cores are cylinder-shaped samples taken from inside ice sheets. In the water of an ice core, the ratio between ¹⁶O and ¹⁸O helps to work out past temperatures and how much snow accumulated. The heavier one, ¹⁸O, condenses more readily as temperatures fall, while the lighter one, ¹⁶O, needs colder conditions to fall as precipitation. Air bubbles in the ice hold trapped greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, and these also help in working out past climate changes. Antarctic ice cores can reveal climate records covering the past 650,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: What tree rings hold
paragraphs.text: Dendroclimatology is the science of working out past climates from trees, mainly from the properties of their annual rings. Rings are wider when conditions favor growth and narrower when times are hard. The two main factors are temperature and water availability. Tree rings have let scientists estimate many local climates over the previous hundreds to thousands of years. By combining several tree-ring studies, sometimes with other proxy records, they have also estimated past climates for whole regions and for the globe.

paragraphs.heading: Limits and uses
paragraphs.text: Proxy records are not spread evenly over the globe. Like the instrumental record, they are more numerous in the northern hemisphere. Proxies can be combined to produce temperature reconstructions that are longer than the instrumental temperature record. Such reconstructions feed into discussions of global warming and of climate history.
